Dataset title: Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS)
Description: The Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS) is a national survey panel by the U.S. Census Bureau (Census). The purpose of the panel is to collect information on topics such as food and nutrition, transportation, employment, and education and to gather data that can be used to improve and inform future surveys. The panel will consist of individuals and households living across the U.S. who have agreed to be contacted and invited to participate in surveys.

prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey: Public Comment

March 2025
  • Download

In February 2025, the U.S. Department of Commerce issued a request for comments on its proposed implementation of the Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS) in March, April, and May 2025.

AUTHORS
  • Elana Redfield
    Federal Policy Director
  • Lauren J.A. Bouton
    Policy Fellow and Research Data Analyst
CONTACT US ABOUT THIS STUDY
Public Comment

Issue
In January 2025, the Census Bureau’s Household Pulse Survey (HPS) was relaunched with a new longitudinal design as the Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS). HTOPS aims to continue to provide data on the social and economic impact of national events on U.S. households, including a variety of population subgroups. In February 2025, the Commerce Department issued a request for comments on proposed data collections for the March, April, and May HTOPS.

Impact
The HPS was the first Census Bureau survey to directly ask participants about their sexual orientation and gender identity. These questions in are a vital tool for examining the differences in social, economic, physical, and psychological well-being between LGBT and non-LGBT people. The Census Bureau has announced that it will not include gender identity questions in future versions of HTOPS, including the three collections in this comment request.

Summary
Scholars provide the Census Bureau with evidence demonstrating that both sexual orientation and gender identity are relevant and important considerations for the proposed collections. They present social science studies showing how this data collection corresponds with Census Bureau goals in assessing the impacts of current events on various subpopulations. In addition, they highlight evidence supporting the inclusion of sexual orientation and gender identity questions on federal surveys, as described in the 2022 recommendations from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine.

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS)
Description: The Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS) is a national survey panel by the U.S. Census Bureau (Census). The purpose of the panel is to collect information on topics such as food and nutrition, transportation, employment, and education and to gather data that can be used to improve and inform future surveys. The panel will consist of individuals and households living across the U.S. who have agreed to be contacted and invited to participate in surveys.
URL: https://census.gov/programs-surveys/htops.html

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

Let me look for the legal authority, the OMB control number, and response rates.# Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS): Research Report

## Verdict on your description

Your description is basically right, but it's out of date in one important way.

| Element | What I found |
|---|---|
| Title | **Correct.** In OMB paperwork the program is called the "High-Frequency Surveys Program/Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey." |
| Publisher | **Correct.** The U.S. Census Bureau (Department of Commerce) is the primary sponsor. Other federal agencies help fund it and supply questions. |
| Topics | **Correct but incomplete.** Food, transportation, employment and education are covered. So are health, mental health, housing, energy, prices and inflation, the arts, AI use and vaccinations. |
| "To gather data that can be used to improve and inform future surveys" | **Correct.** Testing questions and methods is an official purpose, including research for the decennial census. |
| "The panel will consist of individuals… who have agreed to be contacted" | **Out of date.** This was true in 2025, when HTOPS was a longitudinal panel. **Since March 2026 it has been cross-sectional**, meaning a fresh sample of addresses every two months. Census's own pages say so. |
| What's missing | HTOPS is the **direct successor to the Household Pulse Survey (HPS, 2020–2024)** and the Census Household Panel (CHP, 2023–2024). It is labeled an **experimental data product**. |
| URL | **Works.** The official address is `https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/htops.html`. That page is mostly for survey participants. **The actual data and documentation are on the Household Pulse Survey pages** (see Section 6). |

## 1. Publisher and partners

- **Publisher:** U.S. Census Bureau, Demographic Programs (the contact email is addp.htops@census.gov). Phone: 1-888-595-1334, weekdays 8am–5pm ET.
- **Partner agencies** listed for the June 2025 collection: BLS, Bureau of Transportation Statistics, CDC, Department of Defense, Energy Information Administration, HUD, FDA, three HHS offices (Administration for Community Living, ASPE, Surgeon General), the Maternal and Child Health Bureau, NCES, NCHS, the CDC's immunization center (NCIRD), the National Endowment for the Arts, NIOSH, USDA's Economic Research Service and Food and Nutrition Service, and the White House Council of Economic Advisers. The partners vary from one collection to the next.

## 2. Legal authority and mandate

- **Collection authority:** Title 13 of the U.S. Code. The Federal Register notices from 2025 and 2026 cite §§141, 182 and 193. The OMB filings cite §§8(b), 141, 182 and 193. **The HTOPS landing page contradicts itself:** one FAQ cites §§131, 141, 182, 193 and 196, another cites §§141, 182 and 193. Worth noting if you're doing citation work.
- **Confidentiality:** Title 13 protections. Privacy Act records notices COMMERCE/Census-3 (Demographic Survey Collection) and COMMERCE/Census-5 (Decennial Census Programs). Each public file passes Census Disclosure Review Board review.
- **Participation is voluntary.** The legal "affected public" is households.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act clearance:** OMB control number **0607-1029**. This is the same number the Household Pulse Survey used. The Census Household Panel had its own number, 0607-1025.
  - **The expiration date conflicts.** The landing page says 09/30/2028. The OMB approval of 7/13/2026 (for the July, September and November 2026 collections) lists 07/31/2029.
  - Approved burden is 162,768 responses and 54,202 hours per year. The February 2026 notice puts it at 13,564 responses per collection.
  - Each new set of collections goes through a Federal Register notice and a 30-day public comment period, which you can follow on reginfo.gov.
- **There is no specific law requiring HTOPS.** OMB filings describe the program as "a natural progression from the creation of the Household Pulse Survey," run under general Title 13 authority.

## 3. History

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| Apr 2020 | The Household Pulse Survey launches to measure COVID-19's impacts in near real time. It was online, cross-sectional and experimental. |
| Jun 29, 2023 | OMB approves the Census Household Panel. It samples 75,001 addresses from Census's Master Address File, aiming for about 15,000 panelists. |
| Sep 12–Oct 10, 2023 | CHP recruitment: $5 prepaid incentive, $20 for completing the baseline survey, data collected on Qualtrics. |
| Mar–Apr 2024 | 30,000 more addresses are added to the panel (105,001 total). |
| Sep 16, 2024 | The last cross-sectional HPS phase (4.2) ends. Final release Oct 3. Census announces a move to a longitudinal design. |
| Oct and Dec 2024 | Two transitional longitudinal HPS collections. |
| Jan 2025 | HTOPS launches, absorbing the HPS and CHP. OMB clearance came Jan 15, 2025. |
| Feb 2025 | After Executive Order 14168, Census asks OMB for a "non-substantive change" to **delete the gender identity questions** (reported by NPR and the Williams Institute). HPS data pages were briefly taken offline during a government-wide website purge, then restored under a court order. |
| Apr 15, 2025 | Sample expanded to about 30,000 households so results can be published below the national level. The first release, late April, covered Feb 21–Mar 7, 2025 and was national only. |
| 2025 | Public files posted for the February, April and June 2025 collections. OMB also approved collections for March, May, August, September, October and December 2025. |
| Mar 26, 2026 | April 2025 data released with smaller-area detail, about 11 months after collection. |
| Mar 2026 | **Switch to a cross-sectional design.** The March 13–30, 2026 sample covered about 136,000 addresses and supports estimates for the nation, the 4 Census regions and the 10 largest metro areas. |
| Sep 10 / Sep 24, 2026 | March 2026 public file **reissued with corrected weights**. The original population controls wrongly included group quarters (such as dorms and prisons), which HTOPS doesn't survey. Tables were updated Sep 24. |
| Jul–Nov 2026 | Collections approved for July, September and November 2026. A methods statement for July 2026 exists. |

## 4. Methodology (key points for data scientists)

- **Sampling frame:** Census's Master Address File (January 2025 version). Addresses are grouped into "high-response" and "low-response" strata. The grouping uses Census's internal Demographic Frame (administrative and third-party records, not public), the 2024 Planning Database and the 2024 Community Resilience Estimates (a social vulnerability flag). Low-response groups are oversampled.
- **2026 sample size target:** a 9% coefficient of variation for an estimate of 15% in each region and each of the top 10 metro areas, assuming a 10% response rate. That works out to 136,000 addresses.
- **How data are collected:**
  - Up to three mailed invitations, plus outbound phone follow-up and automated reminder calls.
  - Responses are taken online through Census's CENTURION system, or by phone through inbound calls.
  - In 2025, panelists were invited by email and text.
- **Weighting:** raked to American Community Survey controls (the 2023 1-year division-level totals in 2025).
- **Response rates are low.** For June 2025 (panel era):
  - Unweighted: 13.6% completed the baseline and 25.6% of those answered in June, about **3.5% overall**.
  - Weighted: 16.0% and 27.5%, about **4.4% overall**.
  - Census says it will do a nonresponse bias analysis.
- **Table quirk:** the detailed tables show frequency counts that include a "Did not report" category. Census warns users to choose percentage denominators deliberately.
- **Comparability breaks:**
  - Three different designs: cross-sectional HPS (2020–2024), longitudinal HTOPS (Oct 2024–2025), cross-sectional HTOPS (2026 on).
  - Geography keeps changing: national only, then subnational for April 2025, then regions plus top 10 metros.
  - Reference periods change. For example, "difficulty paying expenses in the last 7 days" (June 2025) became "in the last two months" (March 2026).
  - Gender identity has been gone since 2025. I couldn't confirm whether the sexual orientation question is still asked.
- **File naming:** collections use a YYMM code; March 2026 is "HTOPS HPS 2603."

## 5. Data products

- **Public use microdata files** in CSV and SAS, 10–20 MB each. Census says HPS releases came with a replicate weight file and data dictionary. Check whether each HTOPS release does too.
- **Detailed tables and standard error tables** for most releases.
- **Supporting documents:** methods statements ("Source and Accuracy"), user notes, questionnaires, background documentation.
- **OMB packages on reginfo.gov** are a valuable extra record. They include supporting statements and questionnaires, including ones for collections that never got a public data release.
- An ASA report from 2025 noted that HTOPS data at first came out only as microdata. Tables appeared later.

## 6. Notes for preservationists and data librarians

- **The data are scattered across Household Pulse Survey URLs**, not under /htops:
  - `census.gov/data/datasets/time-series/demo/hhp/2025.html` and `.../2026.html` (public files)
  - `census.gov/data/tables/time-series/demo/hhp/2026.html` (tables)
  - `www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/demo/technical-documentation/hhp/` (documentation PDFs)
  - `census.gov/programs-surveys/household-pulse-survey/technical-documentation/user-notes/`
- **Corrected files replace the originals at the same address.** The March 2026 file is an example. Capture each version with its date.
- **There's precedent for takedowns.** The February 2025 removal of HPS pages shows the material is vulnerable. Federal Register notices, OMB filings and Williams Institute public comments are useful outside records of how the content changed.
- **Not all collections appear to have public files.** OMB approved roughly 10 collections in 2025, but the 2025 data page lists files for only three (February, April, June). The Census-only "stakeholder" modules from alternating months may never be released.
- I couldn't check data.gov or ICPSR listings because I hit my search limit. Check those directly.

## 7. Users

- **Federal partner agencies** use it for program monitoring: food sufficiency (USDA), transportation (BTS), energy (EIA), health and vaccination (CDC/NCHS), arts participation (NEA), economic conditions (CEA).
- **Census internal teams** use it for questionnaire testing and decennial census research, such as the Census Barriers, Attitudes and Motivators Survey (CBAMS).
- **State and local governments, researchers, journalists and advocates** carry over from the HPS user base. The Williams Institute, for example, relied on it for LGBT data.

## 8. Public benefits

- Near-real-time readings on emerging problems (inflation stress, food insufficiency, mental health, energy costs, AI use) that standard annual surveys can't catch.
- A probability sample drawn from the Master Address File, which is a stronger basis than opt-in web panels. It can also be linked to administrative records inside Census.
- Less burden on respondents and a quick way to test questions before they go into major surveys.
- Free public microdata.

## 9. Concerns for policy watchers

- **Ongoing experimental status and very low response rates** (a 2025 cumulative rate around 4%) raise the risk of nonresponse bias.
- **Releases have been slow**, which undercuts the "pulse" purpose. April 2025 data came out in March 2026.
- **Questions can be removed without public comment.** Gender identity was dropped through a non-substantive change request. The Williams Institute found that 83% of federal SOGI removals were made this way.
- **Frequent redesigns make it hard to build long-term trends** from HPS through HTOPS.
- **Ways to get involved:** comment on the 30-day Federal Register notices for control number 0607-1029, and track the approval expiration dates.

**Gaps to keep in mind:** the newest methods statements were PDFs I couldn't open. Their details (2026 response rates, final weighting steps) came from excerpts. I also couldn't confirm the exact public-file release dates for each 2026 collection.

HTOPS rates High Risk on four of the six categories (Data Quality, Statutory Context, Staffing and Funding, Policy) and Moderate on the other two. The approval it needs to collect data is current through 2029, so collection isn't at immediate risk of stopping. The risks are that it rests on weak legal ground, it's already been changed for political reasons, and its data is getting slower and less detailed.

**Corrections to my earlier report:**
- **Court order:** I said the Household Pulse Survey (HPS) pages were restored "under a court order." That was wrong. The *Doctors for America* order applied only to HHS, CDC and FDA. Census pages went offline from about January 31, 2025 and came back without a court order, and NPR reported Census made no public statement about it (NPR, Feb 12, 2025).
- **Landing page:** The HTOPS page now says "survey," not "panel," and "the survey sample consists of individuals and households." That matches the 2026 switch to a fresh sample for each collection.

**Staffing tracker:** The tracker you suggested (usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com) loads its numbers dynamically and posts a notice that it will be archived on December 31, 2025, so I couldn't get usable figures from it. Staffing numbers below come from AFGE, the American Statistical Association (ASA), Government Executive and the Congressional Research Service (CRS).

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability → **Moderate Risk**

**Evidence pointing to higher risk:**
- In early February 2025, Census removed HPS data and documentation and the FTP downloads stopped working. This followed Executive Order 14168 and the related OPM memo (Williams Institute brief, Feb 2025; NPR, Feb 12, 2025). NPR said it was "not clear if any data tables ended up getting permanently deleted."
- The October 2024, December 2024 and February 2025 public files each "omitted" variables, which were posted separately as "Supplemental Files." Census doesn't say which variables these are, and given when it happened, they may be the gender identity items.
- The March 2026 file was reissued on September 10, 2026 with corrected weights, replacing the original at the same address. The original is no longer on the page.

**Evidence pointing to lower risk:**
- The data pages currently list every year from 2020 to 2026, with full public files for each 2024 cycle and for the February, April and June 2025 collections (census.gov HPS dataset pages).
- The omitted variables are still downloadable in the supplemental files.

**Why Moderate:** All the files are online now. But the 2025 takedown already happened once, variables have been split out of the main files, and corrected files replace originals without keeping the old version. Each of those means some data elements were pulled from their original files, which fits Moderate. This is close to "No Known Issue"; I chose Moderate because of the takedown precedent.

## 2. Future Data Availability → **Moderate Risk** (close to High)

**Evidence pointing to higher risk:**
- **Skipped and postponed collections:**
  - No data was collected in July 2025 "to allow for operational updates" (90 FR 20272, May 13, 2025).
  - The March 2025 content was moved to May, and the May content was put off with no new date (FR 2025-05093, March 2025).
- **Shutdown:** The October 1–November 12, 2025 government shutdown "disrupted" HTOPS (Census Roadmap operations tracker).
- **Long release delays:**
  - June 2025 data came out April 23, 2026, about 10 months after collection.
  - April 2025 data came out March 26, 2026, about 11 months after collection.
  - For comparison, HPS used to release data about 2–3 weeks after collection ended.
- **Collections with no public data:** Only three 2025 collections have public files (February, April, June). The August, September, October and December 2025 collections were approved but have nothing published. August 2025 is now more than a year old.

**Evidence pointing to lower risk:**
- The OMB approval (control number 0607-1029) is active and current. The July, September and November 2026 collections were approved in July 2026, with a non-substantive change approved September 1, 2026 (reginfo.gov ICR 202608-0607-001). The listed expiration is 2028–2029.
- Collection continues, with Federal Register notices on February 9 and June 4, 2026.

**Why Moderate:** The approval is current and collection is still happening, which keeps this out of High. But there are several missed or postponed collections and releases running 10–11 months late. If the August–December 2025 data never comes out, this should be raised to High.

## 3. Data Quality → **High Risk**

**Evidence:**
- **Frequency is down.** HPS collected every two weeks or every four weeks from 2020 to 2024. HTOPS collects every other month, with gaps.
- **Timeliness is much worse.** Releases went from about 2–3 weeks after collection to about 10–11 months.
- **Geographic detail is down.**
  - HPS gave estimates for all 50 states plus DC and 15 metro areas.
  - HTOPS in 2025 gave national results, then the 9 Census divisions and top 10 metro areas.
  - HTOPS in 2026 gives the nation, 4 regions and 10 metro areas. There are no state estimates.
- **Topic coverage is down.** Gender identity was removed in 2025. The Census Barriers, Attitudes and Motivators Survey (CBAMS) was cancelled and some of its questions were moved into HTOPS. Census Roadmap expects the result to be "less comprehensive" than CBAMS, particularly on race and ethnicity.
- **Accuracy problems.**
  - The overall response rate was about 3.5–4.4% in June 2025.
  - The March 2026 weights had to be corrected because they wrongly included people in group quarters (dorms, prisons and similar).
  - The design has changed three times (cross-sectional, then longitudinal, then cross-sectional again), which breaks trend lines.

**Why High:** Granularity, timeliness and frequency have all already been reduced. These aren't hypothetical risks.

## 4. Statutory Context → **High Risk**

**Evidence:**
- **Legal authority is general.** It rests on Title 13 §§141, 182 and 193 (§8(b) in some filings). §182 lets the Secretary conduct surveys as "necessary" but doesn't require any of them. There is no law that requires HTOPS or HPS, and Census calls it an "experimental endeavor" (91 FR 5705; FR 2026-11172).
- **No program depends on it.** I found no state or federal program that needs HTOPS data to operate. Partner agencies (USDA, BTS, EIA, CDC, NEA and others) use it, but they aren't required to.
- **Partial substitutes exist.** These include the Current Population Survey (CPS) and its supplements, the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS), the American Community Survey (ACS) and the Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking (SHED). None is as fast or as flexible across topics.
- **Census is cutting non-required work.** Its FY2026 budget justification commits to having "eliminated functions that are not statutorily mandated or core to the Bureau's mission" by the end of FY2026 (Government Executive, July 2025).
- **One factor cuts the other way.** USDA ended the Household Food Security Report in September 2025, and HTOPS's food sufficiency questions are now one of the few remaining federal measures of food hardship. Experts call it a "poor substitute" (Investigate Midwest, Oct 16, 2025).

**Why High:** The authority is vague, no program requires the data, it's labeled experimental, and the agency has said it will eliminate functions not required by law. That's the High Risk profile.

## 5. Staffing and Funding → **High Risk**

**Evidence:**
- **Staff losses:**
  - About 1,300 Census employees took deferred resignation, voluntary separation or early retirement in 2025 (AFGE Council 241 via AP and Government Executive). The bureau had about 13,230 employees in September 2024 (OPM figures cited by Government Executive).
  - ASA estimates a 15% staff loss since FY2024, with 18 vacancies among top leaders and their staff (ASA, *The Nation's Data at Risk 2025*; AP).
- **Leadership removed:**
  - Director Santos resigned on February 14, 2025, partway through his term.
  - In September 2025, the career acting director (Ron Jarmin) was replaced by George Cook, a political appointee who is also chief of staff to the Commerce Under Secretary for Economic Affairs. Cook doesn't obviously meet the legal qualifications for the job, according to NPR, AP and CRS.
- **Funding:**
  - The Current Surveys and Programs account went from $328.5M (FY2025) to $318.5M enacted (FY2026), and the FY2027 request is $288.5M, down 9.4% (COSSA).
  - The FY2027 request cuts **Current Demographic Statistics** by $21.0M, 89 full-time staff and 170 positions, leaving $72.5M. That's about a 22% cut (Census Project summary of the FY2027 budget justification). This is the demographic survey area HTOPS most likely falls under, though I couldn't confirm the exact budget line.
  - The budget proposes merging Census, BLS and BEA.
- **Operational limits:** A hiring freeze and a requirement that the Commerce Secretary approve contracts over $100,000 created a backlog of more than 3,000 requests (ASA, citing the Washington Post).

**Why High:** Census meets three separate High Risk thresholds: 1,000 or more staff lost, leadership removed, and a proposed cut of more than 20% to the relevant program.

## 6. Policy → **High Risk**

**Evidence:**
- **Questions removed under an executive order.** Following Executive Order 14168, Census removed the gender identity questions through a "non-substantive change" request, which avoids public comment (NPR, Feb 21, 2025). The Williams Institute confirms Census "will not include gender identity questions in future versions of HTOPS" (Williams Institute public comment, March 2025).
- **Takedown.** Census removed HPS data and documentation to comply with the OPM "gender ideology" memo (Williams Institute; NPR).
- **Other changes in line with Administration priorities:**
  - CBAMS was cancelled.
  - Census was told to eliminate functions not required by law.
  - A political appointee now runs the bureau.
  - A Census/BLS/BEA reorganization has been proposed.
  - The related USDA food security report was ended after USDA called it "redundant, costly, politicized."

**Why High:** The questionnaire has already been changed in direct response to a presidential action, and those changes were approved through the non-substantive change route.

---

## Summary of Risk Levels

- **Historical Data Availability:** Moderate Risk
- **Future Data Availability:** Moderate Risk
- **Data Quality:** High Risk
- **Statutory Context:** High Risk
- **Staffing and Funding:** High Risk
- **Policy:** High Risk

**What would change these ratings:**
- If the August–December 2025 collections are never published, or the approval lapses, Future Data Availability should move to High.
- If a Senate-confirmed, qualified director is appointed and Congress rejects the demographic survey cuts, Staffing and Funding could drop to Moderate.
- **Preservation priority:** Archive the 2026 files now, keeping each version with its date, since corrected files replace the originals.
